background.definition: Superficial thrombophlebitis (STP) is a usually benign and self-limited inflammatory process of the superficial veins, most often of the legs and not always involving thrombosis. It is also commonly called phlebitis.

list.listitem: The exact incidence of STP is not known. It is felt to be more common than DVT, which is estimated to be about 1 per 1000 people annually.
STP occurs in about 0.68 per 1000 pregnancies (95% CI, 0.48-0.88).
STP occurs in 20% of patients with peripheral vascular catheters.
Among nearly 13,000 patients referred for venous duplex examinations, 11% had acute venous thrombosis and 186 (1.5% of all patients, 13% of patients with thromboses) had STP.
Most patients (60%-80%) had STP localized in the great saphenous vein, and it was bilateral in 5% to 10% of the cases.
STP can occur spontaneously in patients with varicose veins (50%-93%) or in pregnant or postpartum patients.
STP can be a manifestation of an underlying systemic disorder such as thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease) or autoimmune disorders such as Behcet's syndrome.
STP can occur as a complication of IV therapy (chemical, mechanical), IV drug abuse, localized trauma, or localized radiation.
In patients with septic STP from IV catheters, the predominant organisms are roughly Staphylococcus aureus (33%), Escherichia coli (25%), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (12%), and Klebsiella (10%).

Underlying malignancy, especially abdominal cancers such as pancreatic cancer, has been associated with migratory STP (Trousseau's thrombophlebitis) and may occur years before the cancer is diagnosed.
STP may also develop in the breast or penis (Mondor's disease).

A systematic review found it difficult to pool data to assess the demographic features of superficial vein thrombosis and its relation with the occurrence of hypercoagulable states. However, hypercoagulable states are definitely associated with STP and may be similar to that seen in DVT, so the same indications for workup apply.

Vascular endothelial injury results in platelet adhesion forming a hemostatic plug that activates the coagulation pathway. The formation of a hemostatic plug is normally opposed by flow dilution, natural anticoagulants, and thrombolytics.

Thrombophlebitis results when there is vascular endothelial injury, venous flow stasis, or a hypercoagulable state (Virchow's triad) that causes more coagulants to accumulate and thus more thrombus formation.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Congestive heart failure or respiratory failure
Immobility due to sitting (eg, prolonged car or air travel)
Increasing age, obesity, or laparoscopic surgery

As predisposing risk factors for STP and VTE are similar, the same concepts of prevention apply: avoid tobacco use, increase movement.
For patients requiring long-term intravascular catheters, close observation with periodic flushing and replacement is recommended.

Although STP occurred in nearly 20% of patients with peripheral IV catheters, the risk did not seem to increase in patients whose catheters were left in place for more than 3 days. As replacing IV catheters is painful and has associated costs, policies mandating routine replacement after 3 days should be re-evaluated.
Treat varicose veins.
Prevent extension and/or recurrence by removing or treating identified risk factors if possible and by managing varicose veins.

Usually multiple nodular lesions, not over a vein; histopathologic diagnosis by biopsy

Edema of calf or leg, deep venous cords; positive Doppler ultrasound

list.listitem: The patient usually presents with localized pain (100%) and swelling (46%).
Over time a firm cord may develop that can persist for months.
Use the Wells criteria for clinical criteria to identify patients at highest risk of DVT.
The presence of fever and/or chills suggests septic/suppurative thrombophlebitis (often a complication of IV cannulation).
Each patient should be carefully examined for involvement of the saphenofemoral junction because there is an increased risk for DVT in STP patients.
About 23% of patients with STP have clinically occult DVT.

Diagnostic compression ultrasound should be performed in the patient with involvement above the knee, risk for DVT, involvement of the saphenofemoral junction, or proximal migration of a distal STP, and if the patient is not responding to conservative management.
Underlying conditions (eg, thrombophilia, malignancy) should be sought in patients with idiopathic, migratory, or recurrent STP and in the absence of varicose veins.
A WBC should be done if there is suspicion of infection.
Histologic diagnosis by biopsy may be necessary when the diagnosis is in question.
An ultrasonographic report of involvement of the superficial femoral vein indicates DVT, and the word "superficial" should not imply STP.
Suspect STP in a patient who presents with localized pain, redness, and swelling, usually in the leg.
The diagnosis of STP is based on the history and finding inflammation localized over a superficial vein.
Clinically categorize patients as those with STP associated with small localized varicosities, those not associated with varicosities, and those with proximal (upper thigh) or extensive disease.
Use the Wells criteria to identify patients at risk for DVT.C
When suspecting DVT, refer the patient for ultrasonography.
Prevent extension and/or recurrence by removing or treating identified risk factors if possible and by ongoing management of varicose veins.
The existing data do not provide strong support for one form of therapy over another in managing patients with superficial thrombophlebitis (STP). C
Patients should be treated with conservative measures such as compression and elevation. A
Anticoagulation with fondaparinux 2.5 mg once daily for 45 days reduces the risk of deep vein thrombosis or extension (NNT=20). A
The goals of therapy are to relieve local symptoms, prevent recurrences, and limit the risk of DVT or pulmonary embolism.
Primary treatment usually includes local heat, elevation, and support stockings.
About 60% of patients with infusion-related, treated with topical diclofenac or oral diclofenac (75 mg twice daily) had symptom relief compared with 20% of patients treated with placebo (NNT = 3).

A trial randomized 3002 patients with acute, symptomatic superficial vein thrombosis to fondaparinux 2.5 mg once daily or placebo for 45 days. Patients given fondaparinux had a significantly lower risk of a composite of death, deep vein thrombosis, or symptomatic extension (0.9% vs 5.9%, p < 0.001, NNT = 20). The risk of pulmonary embolism or DVT was also lower (0.2% vs 1.3%, p < 0.001, NNT = 90).
A Cochrane review also concluded that fondaparinux 2.5 for at least 4 weeks was appropriate therapy for superficial thrombophlebitis of the legs.
Septic thrombophlebitis should be promptly treated with antibiotics that cover staph and Gram negatives.
No data exist that show which group of patients would be likely to benefit.

Surgical management may be considered for severe cases involving very large varicosities, those patients with involvement close to the saphenofemoral junction, recurrent STP, or symptomatic STP that lasts more than 2 weeks with the goal of preventing local recurrence and extension.

In a randomized trial, there was no difference between simple flush ligation and complete stripping in the rates of DVT; simple flush ligation was associated with a somewhat higher risk of extension (NNT 20).
Suppurative STP frequently requires surgical intervention for persistent infection or abscess.
Patients should remain ambulatory when possible.
Remove IV catheter device if it is suspected of causing a STP.
Compression and elevation of the affected limb are recommended. A Cochrane review concluded that wearing elastic strockings were useful.
Therapeutic-dose anticoagulation, when used, should be maintained for at least 4 weeks. B
There is a small (under 10%) but significant association between STP and DVT.B
Most cases resolve in 1 week, but about 10% of cases with greater saphenous vein involvement extend into the deep venous system, which becomes a source of PE.B
More distal STP (except upper extremity STP) should be carefully followed clinically and repeat ultrasonography performed if proximal progression is noted. B
STP is generally a benign, self-limited disease.

Patients who are more likely to have complicated disease include those with bilateral disease, age more than 60 years, male gender, history of DVT, immobility, systemic infection, and involvement of the greater saphenous vein.

Lower extremity STP is not always as benign and self-limited as previously thought. Extension into the deep venous system occurred in about 10% of patients (0.75%-40%), the majority from the greater saphenous vein.
Most cases of uncomplicated STP respond to conservative management in 7 to 10 days, but some cases may take weeks to resolve.
Extension into the deep venous system occurs in about 2% of patients treated with anticoagulation and 3% treated surgically.
Patients should be followed closely to assess for proximal extension.
Little data exist, but it is reasonable and prudent to use duplex scanning in reassessing patients with risk factors for complicated disease.

Patients treated with anticoagulants because of proximal extension but without DVT on ultrasonography should have a repeat scan at 4 to 6 weeks and therapy stopped if there is no DVT or proximal extension.
More distal STP (except upper extremity STP) should be carefully followed clinically and repeat ultrasonography performed if proximal progression is noted.
